requirements: Distribute incoming HTTP requests across multiple backend server instances
Maintain low latency for request processing and response
Achieve fairness in request distribution among servers with different capacities and workload costs
Support health-aware routing by adapting to server performance changes in real-time
Handle request spikes and overload scenarios gracefully to minimize dropped requests
Include operational simplicity and maintainability as the system scales to thousands of servers
Enable dynamic weighting or prioritization of backend servers based on metrics
Support fallback or rerouting mechanisms before dropping requests
Optimize for latency percentiles (median, 95th, 99th) and dropped request rates
assumptions: Backend instances vary in processing power and request cost can be highly variable
Metrics such as average request latency, number of outstanding connections, and queue lengths are available or can be collected per server in near real-time
Load balancer can maintain up-to-date state on server load metrics with low overhead
Network delays and slow start effects are minimal or can be mitigated
Dropping requests is a failure mode to avoid but might be unavoidable under peak overload

alternatives.name: Round Robin
advantages: Works well when servers and request costs are uniform
disadvantages: Does not account for variance in server power or request cost
Can cause imbalanced load and overload on weaker servers
High dropped request rates under load

alternatives.name: Weighted Round Robin
advantages: Distributes requests proportional to predefined server capacity
Improves fairness when server weights are accurate
disadvantages: Requires manual or offline calibration of server weights
Weights hard to maintain or estimate accurately in dynamic environments
Static weights do not adapt to changing server health or load

alternatives.name: Dynamic Weighted Round Robin (based on latency)
advantages: Weights adapt dynamically using observed server latency
Accounts for changes in server performance over time
Improves load distribution fairness compared to static weights
disadvantages: Latency as a proxy for capacity may be noisy or lagging
Additional complexity in collecting and computing weights
Still does not track per-server outstanding load precisely

alternatives.name: Least Connections
advantages: Dynamically balances load by assigning new work to servers with least outstanding requests
Effective under high variance in request costs and server power
Better handling of overload and lower dropped requests than round robin
disadvantages: Does not consider server response latency explicitly
Can cause suboptimal latency for tail requests
Queues full across all servers can still lead to drops

alternatives.name: PEWMA (Peak Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) Latency-based
advantages: Optimizes for latency by prioritizing fastest and least-loaded servers
Smoothly adapts to performance changes using EWMA
Improves median and tail latency compared to least connections
disadvantages: More complex to implement and tune (multiple parameters)
May reduce overall utilization leading to more dropped requests under heavy load
Requires continual performance data and careful parameter configuration

failure_modes: All backend server queues full causing request drops
Latency measurement lag causing suboptimal routing decisions
Incorrect server weight estimations causing imbalance
Network or metric collection failures leading to stale server state
Overload of specific servers due to uneven request cost or slow servers
Load balancer scaling bottleneck or state synchronization issues

evidence.claim: Round Robin is simple but does not handle server or request variance well, resulting in poor fairness and higher dropped requests under load.
Weighted Round Robin requires manual weights, which are often inaccurate or not maintained, limiting practical effectiveness.
Dynamic Weighted Round Robin adapts weights based on real-time latency metrics, improving fairness dynamically.
Least Connections uses current outstanding request counts and dynamically balances load well, especially under variable request costs.
PEWMA algorithm further improves latency metrics by using EWMA latency and prioritizing fastest servers, albeit at higher complexity and risk of dropped requests.

uncertainties: Real-world network latency and slow start effects on load balancer metrics
Cost and feasibility of collecting timely and accurate latency and connection metrics at large scale
Trade-offs between latency optimization and request drop rate under different traffic loads
Parameter tuning and adaptivity of PEWMA in diverse production scenarios
Interaction between load balancing algorithm and backend health checks or failure recovery

gaps: Quantitative comparison including overhead, scalability, and failure recovery
Impact of network latency and metric staleness on algorithm effectiveness
Operational complexity and tooling requirements for each algorithm
Best practices for fallback and rerouting before dropping requests
Empirical data from production or real workloads
research_questions: How to reliably and scalably collect and aggregate real-time server metrics at scale?
What are the optimal PEWMA parameters for typical web workloads?
How to balance latency improvements against increased dropped requests with complex algorithms?
How do load balancers interact with health check and failure detection mechanisms?
What are the operational cost and complexity trade-offs for each algorithm in production?

research.research_summary: For a production HTTP load balancer that must keep latency low, stay fair under heterogeneous backends, handle health and failure gracefully, and remain operationally simple, the strongest practical baseline is health-aware least outstanding requests / least connections with well-tuned health checks and fallback behavior. AWS documents least outstanding requests as the preferred choice when request complexity or target capacity varies, while round robin is best only when targets and requests are similar. NGINX likewise emphasizes least connections and notes it can incorporate active connections plus response-time information in its least-time variant. The newer Google Prequal work shows that production systems can improve tail latency, errors, and resource use by routing with active probes and delayed-state estimates of latency and requests-in-flight, but it adds probe coordination and algorithmic complexity. AWS guidance and whitepapers also make clear that health checks are a complement, not a substitute, for routing decisions; if all targets are unhealthy some systems may fail open, and routing around failure depends on observability and health detection. In practice, metric staleness and network latency matter: delayed feedback can make sophisticated routing less reliable, which is why production algorithms often prefer directly observable in-flight request counts, conservative smoothing, and fallback to simpler policies when signals go stale or unhealthy. Operationally, the simpler algorithms require less tuning and tooling, while latency-aware algorithms can lower p95/p99 but usually demand extra instrumentation, probing, and careful parameter management. The main design implication is to prioritize a simple default path, then layer in bounded adaptivity: health checks, least-outstanding routing, retry/reroute before drop, and optional anomaly or latency bias only where the measurement pipeline is trustworthy.

evidence.claim: AWS recommends least outstanding requests when request complexity or target capacity varies, round robin when requests and targets are similar, and weighted random with anomaly mitigation to shift traffic away from gray failures or elevated latency.
AWS says a load balancer monitors target health and routes only to healthy targets; when a target becomes unhealthy it stops routing traffic to it and resumes when healthy again.

NGINX documents least connections / least-time as load-balancing methods, with least-time selecting the server with the lowest average response time and lowest number of active connections, taking inflight requests into account.

Google’s Prequal paper reports that active probing plus routing by estimated latency and in-flight requests reduced tail latency, errors, and resource use in production at YouTube and other systems, but it is a more complex design than basic least-connections routing.
AWS guidance for NLB target groups notes fail-open behavior when all targets are unhealthy and emphasizes health checks plus routing failover behavior to improve the chance that connections succeed.
AWS best-practices guidance recommends ELB health checks as a complementary safeguard outside the Kubernetes control plane.
